elements.text:
I had another thought on gihub actions vs travis.

With Travis we can save those minutes by using ccache, so we don't have to pay for building boost on each run.

With gh actions, caching is even more flexible, for system we can cache the dependencies, but for things like blockchain, network etc, we'd have system, database etc cached as well. We'd speed up the runs, and save minutes.

For me, just the faster runs is so much nicer. Github can expire cache based the commit you checked out for a dependency. Requires some crafting, but it can help.

elements.text: Revamping libbitcoin-network. The object model remains close to what's there now, but with some material changes to threading. I put together this simplified model to help me visualize relationships. The main simplification is that derived session and protocol classes are not shown.

text: Revamping libbitcoin-network. The object model remains close to what's there now, but with some material changes to threading. I put together this simplified model to help me visualize relationships. The main simplification is that derived session and protocol classes are not shown.

elements.text: The extensible (yellow) classes are modified by deriving from p2p, overriding the virtual attach methods to attach custom derived sessions, and overriding session attach methods to attach custom derived protocols. This is how libbitcoin-node is constructed (adding transaction and header protocols). Of course, the same can be done in libbitcoin-node, and libbitcoin-server inherits from it (though does not change its protocols).

text: The extensible (yellow) classes are modified by deriving from p2p, overriding the virtual attach methods to attach custom derived sessions, and overriding session attach methods to attach custom derived protocols. This is how libbitcoin-node is constructed (adding transaction and header protocols). Of course, the same can be done in libbitcoin-node, and libbitcoin-server inherits from it (though does not change its protocols).

elements.text:
libbitcoin-network is also the threading engine for libbitcoin-node and libbitcoin-server. Node introduces additional thread pools for parallel validation, though these are isolated. Server introduces one thread per endpoint worker (well isolated within libbitcoin-protocol).

This rework dramatically simplifies the threading model, so that we are operating on one dedicated thread per socket/channel. While the implementation remains entirely asynchronous, this will eliminate a lot of complexity and resolve certain issues in our use of boost::asio. It will also reduce our DOS attack surface to almost nothing. I expect it will also finally resolve the shutdown hang (deadlock). If it resurfaces, it will certainly be much easier to troubleshoot.

We may possibly experience a performance hit, as we will not be queueing up arbitrary amounts of work when our processing speed is out of sync with network speed. However, this is the DOS vector. If there's a material hit I would create a managed work buffer, dropping outbound messages or blocking inbound messages as necessary (which is how we manage ZeroMQ buffering).

elements.text: Note that in the model, 'protocol' (actually one derived class per protocol semantic) receives and originates all p2p messages (apart from explicit broadcasts). Each protocol subscribes to the message type(s) of interest. This is part of the elegance of the design. Each derived protocol class entirely encapsulates the semantic (such as compact blocs, ping/pong, headers, txs, blocks, etc.). These are versioned and  are attached independently on each channel (by the session), conforming to the negotiated protocol version of the channel. They are very simple and clearly document each independent protocol.

So custom protocol work is almost entirely isolated to a custom protocol derived class.

elements.text: After getting about half way through this work I found in boost documentation a resolution to the main issue we had with socket write composition. So with a shared threadpool of any size we can still ensure order on each channel.
I’ve also been able to eliminate the execution of message handlers under lock, which eliminates the deadlock hazard.
And I’m finally implementing the DOS protection strategy that has been envisioned for some time. This borrows from lessons learned working from ZeroMQ.

After getting about half way through this work I found in boost documentation a resolution to the main issue we had with socket write composition. So with a shared threadpool of any size we can still ensure order on each channel.

I’ve also been able to eliminate the execution of message handlers under lock, which eliminates the deadlock hazard.

And I’m finally implementing the DOS protection strategy that has been envisioned for some time. This borrows from lessons learned working from ZeroMQ.

elements.text: Given that attached protocols stop any channel that fails to comply with its expected semantics, the only DOS risk is in unbounded expansion of per-channel work queues.

elements.text: This can happen when a peer requests large amounts of data but fails to accept it quickly. It can also happen when a peer sends more work than the network can process. Currently this work accumulates on the opaque asio work queue. So memory consumption simply grows without measure.

elements.text: ZeroMQ uses transparent and configurable work queues for both send and receive. This is a necessary strategy, and it’s sort of surprising that asio doesn’t natively expose controls on its queue. But as all problems in computer science can be resolved with another layer of abstraction, I’ve created a buffered_socket::socket, which maintains size/count read and write message queues. This will suspend read when the read buffer is full (blocking the peer) and overflow the send queue (drop writes) when the write buffer is full. The latter may cause an interruption of the expected protocol semantics, resulting in a dropped connection, though this is acceptable and unavoidable given the p2p protocol design. The other alternative is to drop the peer.

elements.text: The message queues are thus buried in the socket (as with ZeroMQ), maintaining the simplicity of protocol implementation. Ideally we would want to suspend performing work that could not be sent to a peer, but this at least puts an upper bound on the resources that a peer can consume. It will also be possible to provide a cost metric per incoming message type, to limit peer requests by actual resource consumption, suspending the reader until queued work drops below the configured limit.
